why_trail.why: The handoff's four claims are now my own measurements, and one of them changed how I will scope the work. Findings 1, 2 and 4 are pure prose. Finding 3 is prose plus one line, and the line has a tail: :341's write is bracketed by a save at :340 and a restore at :349-352 that exist ONLY to protect that write. The handoff's close criterion says 'one deleted test-setup line', so the save/restore stays and becomes a no-op that saves and restores the same value -- harmless, but residual dead scaffolding I will report rather than silently widen scope to remove. The other thing I measured that the handoff did not: docs/agents/CREW_CONTEXT.md says python3 has no pytest on this host (measured 2026-08-10); today python3 and py both report pytest 9.1.1, so my check commands can use python3 -- but I confirmed that by running it rather than assuming, because a wrong interpreter reads as a silently green suite.

The correction is now tied to the code by a check rather than by my reading of it: g3-rework3-anchor-check.py asserts from the AST that the helper's executable body reads SPINE_FILE zero times, that its anchor expression names SPINE, and that the module docstring carries no surviving SPINE_FILE-derived-checkout claim while naming the helper the code calls. The check demonstrably fails -- --demo-control runs predicate C against the exact pre-change sentence and flags 'primary checkout it opens work from fresh off `SPINE_FILE'. One thing I had to fix in the check itself is worth recording: assertion A first went red on the HELPER'S OWN DOCSTRING, which narrates the os.environ read #603 deleted. Prose about a deleted read is not a read, so A now scans the executable body only -- the same distinction this whole rework is about, met once more inside my own instrument.

The correction landed, but the control is the real finding of this gate. My first predicate B reported the corrected files clean AND reported the pre-change sentences clean -- because its negative lookahead alternative 'OR at' matched unanchored inside 'point the d[oor at] a different spine', so every stale claim in that neighbourhood was excused. Word-boundary-anchoring the alternatives fixed it, and the control now flags both pre-change sentences by name. This is the third time in this gate's history that an instrument reported zero without being able to report anything else, so I am treating 'run the predicate against the exact text it was written to catch' as mandatory for the sweep in m5-sweep too, not merely good practice.

Deleting the write exposed something the handoff's line-accounting did not: the write was bracketed by 'saved_spine_file = os.environ.get(...)' above it and a four-line restore in the finally below, and those exist ONLY to protect the write I just removed. They are now a no-op that saves a value and hands the same value back. I did NOT remove them. The handoff's close criterion says 'one deleted test-setup line' and its stop conditions forbid any logic change beyond that single write, and removing executable lines is a logic change however provably null -- so the compliant move is to leave them and report them, not to widen scope on my own judgment. This is the same class as the finding the handoff itself is built on (dead scaffolding surviving because nobody enumerated what a change invalidated), one layer deeper, and it is the reviewer's call, not mine. My own check had to learn the distinction too: predicate B initially flagged the restore, so it now separates a setup write of a computed value from a teardown restore of a saved one, and the control proves it still catches the deleted line while ignoring the restore beside it.

Two things happened here that the handoff did not anticipate, and both are the handoff's own thesis biting. FIRST: the handoff said four claims; there are FIVE. tests/test_mcp_adoption.py:172-179, the docstring of _load_mcp_spine_server, carries the identical falsified claim ('reads those from the environment at IMPORT time and raises KeyError without both SPINE_FILE/SPINE_ENGINE set'). My check found it because it scans the whole file rather than the line range I was pointed at. I corrected it. That is a departure from the literal allowed scope, which names ':98-102' in this file -- I made it deliberately: the file is in scope and is NOT on the fenced list, the close criterion demands 0 live invalidated claims in the source tree, and 'scoped my sweep to my edit permission instead of the blast radius' is the exact mistake this rework exists to correct. Fixing four of five and reporting the fifth would reproduce it. SECOND: my first correction restated the false claim in order to retract it ('the reason this used to give ... is void'), and my own predicate flagged it. I could have taught the predicate to excuse retractions; I reworded instead. A sweep that understands negation is a sweep that can be talked out of a finding, and being talked out of findings is how the last two attempts reported zero. The file is now clean of the claim outright, not clean modulo an exemption.

The sweep found three more instances beyond the handoff's four, and HOW each was found is the finding. #5 (tests/test_mcp_adoption.py:172) came from scanning the whole file instead of the line range I was pointed at. #6 (tests/test_mcp_identity.py:18) came from the claim-class predicate: it says 'binds its ambient state ... at server-launch time', which my narrower m2 check could not match, so a phrasing-based trigger caught what an identifier-based one missed. #7 (docs/CHECKLIST_ENGINE_DESIGN.md:295) matched NO predicate at all -- 'at launch from its environment' -- and I found it only by reading the 271-fragment source dump by hand. That is the handoff's instruction 'READ the hits, do not trust the classifier' paying for itself, and it means the honest description of this sweep is 'an instrument that narrows 207254 fragments to 271 a person can read', never 'an instrument that decides'. Accordingly --assert-clean's exit code comes from a per-hit ledger I wrote by reading, not from a predicate, and a hit absent from that ledger REFUSES rather than passes -- so tomorrow's new claim cannot slip through by not being listed. TWO LIVE CLAIMS SURVIVE, both in FENCED files, both reported and untouched per the stop condition: scripts/run_crew.py:468-471 carries finding 4's exact falsified rationale, and tests/test_mcp_lifecycle.py:200's pin message says 'purely on server-launch-time state', which bind-on-open makes loose. This exposes a real conflict in the handoff for the reviewer to rule on: the close criterion demands 0 live invalidated claims in scripts/, but scripts/run_crew.py is both in scripts/ and fenced.
